title: Relativistic Momentum
lead: If conservation of momentum is to hold in every inertial frame, momentum needs a new definition. Relativistic momentum $\kp = \gamma m\ku$ becomes the classical $m\ku$ at low velocities and approaches infinity as $\ku$ approaches $\kc$. The only mass it makes sense to talk about is rest mass, and relativistic momentum is conserved whenever the net external force is zero.
objectives: Explain why the only mass it makes sense to talk about is rest mass.
summary_html:
• The law of conservation of momentum is valid whenever the net external force is zero and for relativistic momentum. Relativistic momentum $\kp$ is classical momentum multiplied by the relativistic factor $\gamma$.
  • $\kp = \gamma m\ku$, where $m$ is the rest mass of the object, $\ku$ is its velocity relative to an observer, and the relativistic factor $\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \frac{\ku^{2}}{\kc^{2}}}}$.
  • At low velocities, relativistic momentum is equivalent to classical momentum.
  • Relativistic momentum approaches infinity as $\ku$ approaches $\kc$. This implies that an object with mass cannot reach the speed of light.
  • Relativistic momentum is conserved, just as classical momentum is conserved.

exercises.prompt: What is the momentum of an electron traveling at a speed $0.985c$? The rest mass of the electron is $9.11\times 10^{-31}\;\text{kg}$.

answer.hint: Multiply the classical momentum $m\ku$ by $\gamma$, which at $0.985c$ is well above 1.

exercises.prompt: How does modern relativity modify the law of conservation of momentum?

answer.solution: The law itself survives: whenever the net external force on a system is zero, its total momentum is conserved, in every inertial frame. What changes is the definition of momentum. Classical momentum $m\ku$ is not conserved in all frames at high velocities, so it is replaced by relativistic momentum $\kp = \gamma m\ku$, which is. At low velocities $\gamma$ is very nearly 1, and the new law becomes the classical one.

exercises.prompt: Is it possible for an external force to be acting on a system and relativistic momentum to be conserved? Explain.

answer.solution: Yes, provided the net external force is zero. Conservation requires only that the external forces add to zero, as in classical physics, so several external forces that cancel leave the total relativistic momentum unchanged. A single unbalanced external force changes the momentum, and then it is not conserved.

exercises.prompt:
What happens when velocities comparable to the speed of light are involved in an observation?
(a) Newton’s second law of motion, $F = ma$, governs the motion of the object.
(b) Newton’s second law of motion, $F = ma$, no longer governs the dynamics of the object.
(c) Such velocities cannot be determined mathematically.
(d) None of the above

answer.solution: Consider what happens to momentum near the speed of light. Classical momentum $m\ku$ is not conserved in all inertial frames at such velocities, and it must be replaced by $\kp = \gamma m\ku$, which grows without limit as $\ku$ approaches $\kc$. A constant force therefore cannot keep producing a constant acceleration, since that would carry the object past $\kc$. So $F = ma$ in its classical form no longer describes the motion, which points to (b); the velocities themselves are perfectly calculable, which rules out (c).

exercises.prompt: Find the momentum of a helium nucleus having a mass of $6.68\times 10^{-27}\;\text{kg}$ that is moving at $0.200c$.

answer.hint: At $0.200c$ the factor $\gamma$ is only slightly above 1, but include it.

exercises.prompt: (a) Find the momentum of a $1.00\times 10^{9}\;\text{kg}$ asteroid heading towards the Earth at 30.0 km/s. (b) Find the ratio of this momentum to the classical momentum. (Hint: Use the approximation that $\gamma = 1 + (1/2)\kv^{2}/\kc^{2}$ at low velocities.)

parts.hint: Multiply $m\ku$ by $\gamma$ from the approximation, and keep enough digits to see the difference from $m\ku$.

parts.part: (b) the ratio to the classical momentum

answer.solution:
(a) $3.000000015\times 10^{13}\;\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$.
(b) Ratio of relativistic to classical momenta equals 1.000000005 (extra digits to show small effects)

exercises.prompt: What is the velocity of an electron that has a momentum of $3.04\times 10^{-21}\;\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$? Note that you must calculate the velocity to at least four digits to see the difference from $c$.

answer.hint: Solve $\kp = m\ku/\sqrt{1 - \ku^{2}/\kc^{2}}$ for $\ku$: square both sides and collect the terms in $\ku^{2}$.

exercises.prompt: (a) Calculate the speed of a $1.00\text{-}\mu\text{g}$ particle of dust that has the same momentum as a proton moving at $0.999c$. (b) What does the small speed tell us about the mass of a proton compared to even a tiny amount of macroscopic matter?

answer.part: (a) the speed of the dust particle
answer.hint: Find the proton’s relativistic momentum first; the dust is so slow that its momentum is classical.
answer.solution:
(a) $1.121\times 10^{-8}\;\text{m/s}$
(b) The small speed tells us that the mass of a proton is substantially smaller than that of even a tiny amount of macroscopic matter!
